source_text: Omnes autem pro multis poni innumera Scripturarum exempla testantur secundum illud: Omnes declinaverunt, simul inutiles facti sunt, et post pauca: Qui devorant - inquit - plebem meam sicut cibum panis [n277] , ostendens ab illis omnibus, quos malum pronuntiaverat operari, hanc plebem fuisse discretam. In Evangelio refertur: Et clamabat omnis populus: Crucifige! Crucifige! [n278] Et tamen generalitate verbi huius nequaquam aut Apostoli aut Nicodemus aut sanctae mulieres includuntur. Hic ipse Apostolus, quos nunc dixit omnes, paulo post multos nominat.
pass_a_gloss: But that all is placed for many innumerable examples of the Scriptures testify according to that: All have declined, they have been made useless together, and after a few: Who devour, he says, my people as the food of bread, showing that this people had been discreted from those all whom he had pronounced to work evil. In the Gospel it is reported: And all the people were crying: Crucify! Crucify! And yet by the generality of this word neither the Apostles nor Nicodemus nor the holy women are in any way included. This Apostle himself, those whom he now said all, a little later names many.

lemmas.lexica: LS exemplum; Blaise Adam as example not transmitter
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: Countless scriptural examples testify that ‘all’ is used for ‘many.’ For example: ‘All have turned aside; together they have become useless.’ A little later he says, ‘They devour my people as a meal of bread’ (Psalm 14:3–4; LXX/Vulgate 13:3–4), showing that this people was distinct from all those whom he had declared evildoers. The Gospel reports: ‘And all the people cried out, “Crucify! Crucify!”’ (Luke 23:21; Mark 15:13; compare Matthew 27:22–23). Yet the universality of this expression certainly includes neither the apostles, nor Nicodemus, nor the holy women. This same apostle shortly afterward calls ‘many’ those whom he now calls ‘all’ (Romans 5:19).

choices.why: Adam as example to later sinners, Julian's alternative to tradux.
Julian's name for the doctrine he attacks: evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

variants.reading: Source note 278 prints Matthew 27:33, the arrival at Golgotha; the relevant parallel to the cry “Crucify” is Matthew 27:22–23. The source reading is recorded here and the parallel is corrected in the text.
